name: Python
description: Semantics, the data model, idioms and the gotchas that bite in interviews and production.

modules.name: Core Semantics
modules.description: Names, binding, scope and the rules that explain most surprising Python behaviour.

cards.prompt: In Python, what does assignment (`x = y`) actually do?
cards.answer: It binds the **name** `x` to the same object `y` refers to. It never copies the object.
cards.explanation: Python has names and objects, not boxes holding values. Assignment rebinds a name in a namespace; the object is untouched. This single rule explains aliasing, mutable default arguments, and why `a = b` on a list means both names see the same list.

resources.title: Python docs — Execution model: naming and binding

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

print(add(1))
print(add(2))
cards.explanation: Default arguments are evaluated **once**, when the `def` statement executes — not per call. The same list object is reused on every call that omits the argument. The fix is `bucket=None` plus `if bucket is None: bucket = []`.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
fns = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fns])
cards.explanation: Closures capture the **variable**, not its value at creation time. By the time the lambdas run, the comprehension has finished and `i` is 2. Bind eagerly with a default argument — `lambda i=i: i` — to capture the current value.

resources.title: Python FAQ — Why do lambdas defined in a loop with different values all return the same result?

cards.prompt: `is` vs `==`
cards.answer: `is` compares identity (same object); `==` compares value via `__eq__`.

points: Correct for values: numbers, strings, containers

cards.explanation: Use `is` only for singletons. `x is 1000` may be False while `x == 1000` is True, because CPython interns only small integers (-5..256) and some strings. Never rely on interning for correctness.

cards.prompt: Python resolves names in the order Local → ___ → Global → Builtins.
cards.answer: Enclosing
cards.explanation: The LEGB rule: Local (current function), Enclosing (any outer function), Global (module), Builtins. `global` rebinds at module level; `nonlocal` rebinds in the nearest enclosing function scope.

cards.prompt: Which values are falsy in Python?
cards.answer: `False`, `None`, zero of any numeric type, and empty containers/strings — plus any object whose `__bool__` returns False or whose `__len__` returns 0.
cards.explanation: `if x:` calls `bool(x)`, which tries `__bool__` then `__len__`, defaulting to True. That is why `if my_list:` is idiomatic for 'not empty', but `if x is not None:` is required when 0 or an empty list are legitimate values.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)
print(a, b, a is b)
cards.explanation: `b = a` binds a second name to the same list. Mutating through either name is visible through both. Copy explicitly with `a[:]`, `list(a)` or `copy.deepcopy` when you need independence.

cards.prompt: What do `*args` and `**kwargs` mean in a signature, and what do `*` and `/` mean on their own?
cards.answer: `*args` collects extra positionals into a tuple, `**kwargs` collects extra keywords into a dict. A bare `*` forces everything after it to be keyword-only; a bare `/` forces everything before it to be positional-only.
cards.explanation: Positional-only (`/`, PEP 570) lets you rename parameters without breaking callers. Keyword-only (`*`, PEP 3102) stops callers passing booleans and flags as unlabelled positionals, which is the single cheapest readability win in an API.

modules.name: Data Model & Objects
modules.description: Dunder methods, classes, descriptors and how Python objects really behave.

cards.prompt: What is the Python data model, and why do dunder methods matter?
cards.answer: It is the set of protocols (`__len__`, `__iter__`, `__getitem__`, `__eq__`, `__enter__`…) that built-in syntax and functions dispatch to. Implementing them makes your object work with `len()`, `for`, `in`, `with`, operators and unpacking.
cards.explanation: Python's syntax is a thin veneer over the data model: `len(x)` is `type(x).__len__(x)`, `a + b` is `type(a).__add__`, `with x:` is `__enter__`/`__exit__`. Building on those protocols is what makes a class feel native rather than bolted on.

resources.title: Fluent Python (Ramalho) — the Python data model

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.answer:
B
['D', 'B', 'C', 'A', 'object']
cards.explanation: Python linearises multiple inheritance with C3: depth-first, left-to-right, but a class never precedes its subclasses. `D.__mro__` is the exact lookup order, and `super()` walks it — which is why cooperative `super()` calls in every class matter with diamonds.

resources.title: Python docs — The Python 2.3 method resolution order

cards.prompt: What does `__slots__` do?
cards.answer: It replaces the per-instance `__dict__` with a fixed array of descriptors — cutting memory per instance substantially and blocking new attributes at runtime.
cards.explanation: A normal instance carries a dict (tens of bytes of overhead plus hashing). `__slots__ = ('x', 'y')` stores attributes in a compact struct instead. The trade-offs: no dynamic attributes, no default `__weakref__` unless declared, and inheritance rules get fiddly.

cards.prompt: `@dataclass` vs `NamedTuple`
cards.answer: Dataclasses are mutable, flexible classes; NamedTuples are immutable tuples with names.

right.title: NamedTuple
points: Is a real tuple — unpacks and indexes
Awkward to extend or add behaviour

cards.explanation: Reach for a NamedTuple for small immutable value records that flow through tuple-shaped APIs; a dataclass for anything with behaviour, defaults or mutation. `frozen=True, slots=True` dataclasses get you close to the best of both.

cards.prompt: You need a resource released even when the body raises. What is the idiomatic Python mechanism, and how do you write one?
cards.answer: A context manager: implement `__enter__`/`__exit__`, or decorate a generator with `@contextlib.contextmanager` and put the cleanup in a `finally`.
cards.explanation: `with` guarantees `__exit__` runs on normal exit, exception, `return` and `break`. Returning True from `__exit__` swallows the exception — almost always wrong unless you mean it. `contextlib.ExitStack` composes an unknown number of them at runtime.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
def gen():
    print('start')
    yield 1
    print('middle')
    yield 2

g = gen()
print('created')
print(next(g))
print(next(g))
cards.answer:
created
start
1
middle
2
cards.explanation: Calling a generator function runs **no** body code — it builds a generator object. The body advances only on each `next()`, up to and including the next `yield`. That laziness is what makes generators memory-flat over huge sequences.

cards.prompt: This decorator works, but something important is lost. What, and how do you fix it?
cards.answer: The wrapper replaces the function's metadata: `add.__name__` is now `'wrapper'` and the docstring is gone. Fix it with `@functools.wraps(fn)` on `wrapper`.
cards.explanation: `functools.wraps` copies `__name__`, `__doc__`, `__module__`, `__qualname__` and `__dict__`, and sets `__wrapped__` so `inspect.signature` can see through the decorator. Without it, introspection, docs tooling and debuggers all lie about your function.

cards.prompt: If you define `__eq__` on a class, what happens to hashing, and what is the contract?
cards.answer: Defining `__eq__` sets `__hash__` to None, making instances unhashable. The contract: equal objects must have equal hashes, and a hash must not change while the object is in a container.
cards.explanation: Python removes the inherited identity hash because it would break the invariant. Either define `__hash__` over the same immutable fields you compare, or use `@dataclass(frozen=True)`, which generates a matching pair for you.

modules.name: Runtime, Async & Performance
modules.description: The GIL, concurrency choices, memory behaviour and where Python time actually goes.

cards.prompt: What is the GIL, and what does it actually prevent?
cards.answer: The Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time in a CPython process. It prevents CPU-bound parallelism across threads — not concurrency, and not parallel I/O.
cards.explanation: Threads still help for I/O: the GIL is released around blocking syscalls and in many C extensions (NumPy, compression, hashing). For CPU-bound work use `multiprocessing`, a C extension that releases the GIL, or the free-threaded build (PEP 703) where available.

cards.prompt: You must fetch 5,000 HTTP endpoints, then run an expensive pure-Python transform on each response. How do you structure the concurrency?
cards.answer: `asyncio` (or a thread pool) for the I/O fan-out, then hand the CPU-bound transform to a `ProcessPoolExecutor`.
cards.explanation: I/O waits release the GIL, so thousands of sockets are cheap with async or threads. The transform is bytecode-bound, so it needs separate processes to use more than one core. `loop.run_in_executor` with a process pool bridges the two halves cleanly.

cards.prompt: This async handler serves one request at a time. Why?
cards.code:
import asyncio, time

async def handle(n):
    time.sleep(1)          # simulate work
    return n * 2

async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(*(handle(i) for i in range(10)))
cards.answer: `time.sleep` blocks the event loop thread, so nothing else can run. Use `await asyncio.sleep(1)`, or push genuinely blocking work to `asyncio.to_thread` / an executor.
cards.explanation: An event loop is cooperative: a coroutine holds the thread until it awaits. Any synchronous blocking call — `time.sleep`, `requests.get`, heavy CPU loops, blocking DB drivers — stalls every other task on that loop.

cards.prompt: List comprehension vs generator expression
cards.answer: `[...]` materialises every element; `(...)` yields them one at a time.

left.title: [x for x in it]
points: Allocates the whole list up front
Faster when you need every element twice

cards.explanation: `sum(x*x for x in range(10**8))` runs in constant memory; the list version tries to allocate gigabytes. Prefer generators for pipelines and single passes, lists when you need random access or multiple traversals.

cards.prompt: Average-case complexity of `d[key]`, `d[key] = v` and `key in d` on a Python dict?
cards.answer: All O(1) on average; O(n) in the pathological collision case.
cards.explanation: CPython dicts are open-addressed hash tables with a compact index array (PEP 509 / 3.6 layout) that also preserves insertion order. Worst case only appears with adversarial or degenerate hashes; string hashing is randomised per process to defend against that.

cards.prompt: Why is this quadratic, and what is the fix?
cards.answer: Strings are immutable, so each `+=` allocates and copies the whole accumulated string — O(n²) total. Use `','.join(parts)` or accumulate into a list and join once.
cards.explanation: CPython has an in-place optimisation when a string has a refcount of one, so this sometimes looks fast — but it is not guaranteed and disappears the moment another name references `out`. `join` computes the final size once and copies each part exactly once.

cards.prompt: Two things are wrong with this error handling. What are they?
cards.answer: A bare `except:` also swallows `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`, and the original traceback is discarded. Catch `Exception` (or the specific type) and log with `logging.exception` or re-raise with `raise ... from err`.
cards.explanation: Bare except catches everything deriving from `BaseException`, so Ctrl-C stops working. Losing the traceback turns a five-minute debug into an afternoon. If you truly cannot handle it, do not catch it.

cards.prompt: In modern Python, `Optional[int]` is written more plainly as `int | ___`.
cards.answer: None
cards.explanation: PEP 604 added the `X | Y` union syntax (Python 3.10+), so `Optional[int]` is `int | None` and `Union[str, bytes]` is `str | bytes`. Type hints are not enforced at runtime — they exist for readers, editors and static checkers such as mypy or pyright.
